source.title: Data Scaling Laws in Imitation Learning for Robotic Manipulation
source.authors: Fanqi Lin; Ying-Dong Hu; Ping-Yue Sheng; Chuan Wen; Jia-Cheng You; Yang Gao

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some figure equations are flattened, so exponent signs are not reliably visible in the extracted text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether scaling relationships generalize to robotic imitation learning, a different modality and training regime from language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The study measures robot-policy generalization scores and action MSE as training data diversity or quantity changes. These are not held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy results. The reported results on model-size comparisons in Section 6 are not power-law fits; the overall success-rate table does not compare scale conditions.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws to robot imitation-learning policy performance (optimality gap, and action MSE in Appendix G.1) against counts of training objects, environments and environment-object pairs. Its own results bear on whether the power-law form carries over to a new training regime (V5). It does not measure language-model pretraining loss, so V1–V4, V6 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that generalization scales roughly as a power law with training objects, environments and env-object pairs, while demonstration count saturates. Diversity matters more than quantity. About 32 env-object pairs with 50 demos each yields around 90% success. Visual-encoder scaling helps but action-model scaling does not.
record.recipe_differences: Uses real-world robot imitation-learning datasets and tester-assigned generalization scores (with action MSE as an alternative), rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy over parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed relationship depends on the scaling dimension and metric: environment/object/pair diversity shows approximate power laws in tester scores, while demonstration count plateaus and action MSE is weaker and can have outliers.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation action MSE tracks real-world score strongly for env-object pairs (Pearson r=−0.98) but weakly for objects (r=−0.73). LoRA has lower MSE yet a worse score (0.72 vs 0.90).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In robot imitation learning, offline loss (action MSE) is an unreliable predictor of closed-loop task performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 6, Table 2: scaling the visual encoder ViT-S/B/L gives scores 0.66/0.81/0.90. Scaling the action U-Net small/base/large gives 0.88/0.90/0.83, with no gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model-size scaling in diffusion robot policies helps for the visual encoder but not the action head (no power-law fit).

record.problems: The main score-based fits use only six data points per fit; the authors say a three-parameter model including irreducible error is not statistically justified with six points. The MSE measure can be anomalous and does not always track real-world performance. The study covers four tasks and uses one policy-learning algorithm.
record.rows_left_out: Section 6, Table 2 compares training strategies and visual-encoder/action-diffusion model sizes, but does not report power-law fits; these results were not included as scaling-law rows. Table 1 reports task success rates for policies trained with the proposed strategy, not results across varying scale conditions.

untested.parts: Scaling with model parameters or compute (Section 6 compares only three sizes, with no fit). Image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning/transfer. Scaling over several orders of magnitude (the fits cover 1–32, about 1.5 decades).
The authors predict 1,191 env-object pairs for a 0.99 score on Mouse Arrangement but explicitly leave verification to future work. In any case this is not language-model loss.
Not tested: no language-model pretraining loss.
Not tested: no shape sweep at fixed parameter count.
Not tested: no comparison of fitting or counting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The data axis here is diversity count (environments/objects), not dataset tokens, and the measure is mainly a tester-assigned score rather than loss; the MSE fits are the closest analogue to loss. Model-size results (Table 2) are declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as missing. The exponents in Figures 5 and 20 are negative; their signs were lost in text extraction.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger language-model runs from small-run loss fits.
Compute-optimal allocation between language-model parameters and tokens.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed language-model parameter count.
Tests robot imitation learning with data and policy-performance measures, not the same held-out pretraining-loss measure. Does not test image/video scaling, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Predictability of language-model downstream task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Does not compare language-model fitting or counting choices, or test whether language-model curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: Diffusion Policy (Pour Water)
rows.operation_detail: Vary total demonstrations with environments and objects fixed.
rows.value: Performance plateaus at 800 demonstrations; for the maximum-demonstration setting, the reported correlation coefficient is −0.62.
rows.note: Authors state there is no clear power-law relationship for demonstration count; performance first rises and then plateaus.
rows.check: The −0.62 is the correlation for the M=16, N=64 setting (64–6400 demos), which the authors call only weakly power-law. Scores plateau near 800 demos and dip at 6400 (Table 7: 7.125 to 6.525). Environment/object diversity is held fixed, which may itself be the bottleneck.

rows.value: Performance plateaus at 800 demonstrations; for the maximum-demonstration setting, the reported correlation coefficient is −0.79.
rows.note: Authors state there is no clear power-law relationship for demonstration count; performance first rises and then plateaus.
rows.check: r=−0.79; the plateau begins around 800 demos (Table 11). Diversity is held fixed and may be the bottleneck.

relationships.condition: Tester-assigned optimality gap, and action MSE, versus number of training objects, environments, or env-object pairs (100% demos), Pour Water and Mouse Arrangement
relationships.reason: Log-log linear fits have |r| of 0.94–0.99 for scores (r1–r6) and about 0.95 for most MSE fits (r7, r9–r12).
relationships.display_finding: Log-log linear fits yielded absolute correlations of 0.94–0.99 for score gaps and about 0.95 for most action-MSE fits.

relationships.condition: Action MSE versus training environments on Pour Water; total demonstration count with diversity fixed
relationships.reason: The MSE fit is weak (r=0.558, outliers; r8). Demonstration-count scaling plateaus near 800 demos with only weak power-law correlation (−0.62, −0.79; r13, r14).
relationships.display_finding: Action MSE fit weakly with r = 0.558, while demonstration scaling plateaued near 800 demonstrations with correlations of −0.62 and −0.79.

relationships.condition: All score fits: six points spanning 1–32 objects/environments/pairs, two-parameter fit without an irreducible term
relationships.reason: The power-law form is shown over only about 1.5 decades, with fits that omit an irreducible error the authors acknowledge exists (Section 4.2 footnote; r1–r6).
relationships.display_finding: Power-law fits covered about 1.5 decades and omitted an acknowledged irreducible error term.
